introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** Describe an incident in which you were involved that brought shame and disgrace to your school.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Opening: the newspaper headline and the narrator's role.
2. Background: the quiz competition and the pressure to win.
3. The temptation: the plan to cheat and the narrator's silence.
4. The incident: discovery in the hall and disqualification.
5. Consequences for the school and the punishment.
6. Lessons learnt and conclusion.

**Model composition (538 words)**

I still remember the Thursday morning when the name of my school, Government Bilingual High School, appeared in the regional newspaper under a headline that made me want to disappear. I was in Upper Sixth, a prefect and a member of the school quiz team, and I was one of the people who brought shame and disgrace on the school that week.

It happened during the inter-school quiz competition held in the regional capital. Our team had won the first two rounds, and the whole school expected us to bring home the trophy. The principal had told us that we carried the reputation of two thousand students on our shoulders, and those words filled us with fear. We were so afraid of losing that we forgot the one thing we had been taught from the first day: that honour matters more than victory.

On the morning of the final, one of my teammates, whom I shall call Ayuk, suggested a plan. He had smuggled two small phones into the hall, hidden in his socks, and proposed that the two of us who sat at the back should search for difficult answers while the others kept the judges busy. I knew it was wrong. A voice inside me said clearly, "Refuse." But I looked at the faces of my friends, thought of the trophy, and said nothing. My silence was my first mistake. It was also my first act of cheating.

The final began well. We answered three questions correctly, and the audience cheered. Then came a question on the history of the African Union, and Ayuk bent forward to read the answer on the screen under the table. At that very moment a supervisor walked down the aisle and noticed the blue light on his face. The hall fell silent. The phone was taken, our papers were checked, and the second phone was found in my bag.

The judges disqualified our school at once and announced the reason through the microphone. A journalist in the front row wrote it all down. The following day, the newspaper reported that students of a leading school had cheated in a competition meant to promote knowledge. Parents telephoned the principal, and students from rival schools sang mocking songs when our bus passed.

The punishment was severe but fair. Ayuk and I were suspended for two weeks and removed from our posts as prefects. The principal summoned us to his office and said, in a quiet voice that hurt more than shouting, "You did not only lose a cup. You lost the trust that took this school fifty years to build."

Yet that painful experience taught me several things. I learnt that cowardice often hides behind the mask of loyalty, and that a true friend is one who dares to say 'no'. I learnt that a defeat honestly earned is better than a victory stolen. In the following term, I wrote a letter of apology to the whole school, and I was allowed to speak at the assembly about what had happened.

Today I look back on that morning with sorrow, but also with gratitude. It destroyed my pride, but it built my character, and I promise never to bring such disgrace again.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Describing the school's good name in general terms instead of 'an incident in which you were involved': the answer must be one particular event with the writer's own part in it (a story, with people, place and time).
